rows.title: Conjecture on the UT-rank of the monoid M_5
rows.record_statement: Let $M_5 = \operatorname{Mon}\langle a,b\mid aba=ba\rangle$ be the one-relation monoid with defining relation $aba=ba$. Its **UT-rank** is the least $n$ such that $M_5$ admits a faithful representation into $\operatorname{UT}_n(\overline{\mathbb{Z}})$. **UT-rank conjecture for $M_5$.** The monoid $M_5$ has UT-rank exactly $4$. This is the remaining question for the UT-tropical embeddings considered here: an embedding into $\operatorname{UT}_4(\overline{\mathbb{Z}})$ is known, but it is not known whether smaller matrices suffice.
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds: M5 embeds in the upper triangular 4×4 matrices over the max-plus semiring on ℤ ∪ {−∞}, and in no smaller size. The new part is the lower bound. Fix the sum of the first and last exponents of a normal form C^α A^β B^γ; the defining relation then forces every entry of the image except the (1,3) entry to be determined, while that one entry can take only linearly many integer values; there are quadratically many normal forms, so two of them collide and no homomorphism into UT_3 is injective (sizes 1 and 2 are handled the same way). The argument uses that the entries are integers: over the real max-plus semiring a faithful UT_3 representation exists, so the statement is specific to ℤ. The upper bound is the source's Lemma 2.9 with one printed entry corrected (B₁₁ = −1); Lean also proves that the matrix as printed (B₁₁ = 1) is not injective. Lean states the conjecture with M5 as a presented monoid, UT_n as the subsemigroup of upper triangular matrices over MinTropical (WithTop ℤᵒᵈ) (proved to be max-plus on ℤ ∪ {−∞}), and an embedding as an injective semigroup homomorphism.

rows.title: The prism B-factorizability conjecture
rows.record_statement:
For a regular graph $G=(V,E)$, call $G$ **B-factorizable** if every saturated monoid element with edge component equal to the graph's characteristic vector belongs to the monoid generated by compatible perfect matchings. A $k$-gonal prism is the graph formed by two $k$-cycles together with corresponding matching edges.

**Prism B-factorizability conjecture.** The graph of every $k$-gonal prism is B-factorizable.

The source reports verification for the 3-dimensional cube and the pentagonal prism by Hilbert-basis calculations, but does not establish the claim for every $k$.
rows.source: Kenji Kashiwabara, “Sports scheduling for not all pairs of teams”, arXiv:0809.3682 (2008).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds for every k ≥ 3: whenever a home-away pattern table for the k-gonal prism (a round-robin style schedule in which only the pairs of teams joined by a prism edge play) admits a fractional compatible schedule, it admits an integral one. The proof starts from Kashiwabara's own Corollary 9, which reduces the question to finding a compatible proper 3-edge-colouring, and then uses three prism-specific steps: the differences along the two rails alternate, the one-turn digraph of the pattern can be spliced into cycles with the right cut parity, and the exclusions on the rungs propagate around the prism to give the colouring. Kashiwabara had verified the cube (k = 4) and the pentagonal prism (k = 5) by Hilbert-basis computation. Lean states Definition 4 of the source literally (the monoid generated by compatible perfect matchings, its saturation, B-factorizability) and proves it for prism k for all k ≥ 3, together with the equivalent statement that the feasible polytope has an integral point when it is non-empty.

rows.title: Preperiod conjecture for extensions of subtraction sets of size at most three
rows.record_statement:
Let $A$ be a finite subtraction set with $|A|\leq 3$, let $S\in\{0,1\}^{\alpha}$ be a seed, and write $p=\operatorname{Per}(A,S)$. An integer of the form $kp+x$ is an **extension** of $A$ for every $k\in\mathbb{N}_+$ and $x\in A$ under the condition stated. **Preperiod-extension conjecture.** If $kp+x$ is an extension of $A$ for all $k\in\mathbb{N}_+$ and $x\in A$, then

$$
\operatorname{PrePer}(A,S)=0.
$$

The statement is the converse of the cited invariant-extension proposition for sets of size at most three. The source notes that it suffices to check $k=1$, and that the converse is not true for nonempty seeds in the unrestricted setting.
rows.source: István Miklós and Logan Post, “Superpolynomial period lengths of the winning positions in the subtraction game”, arXiv:2312.02426 (2023).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds: for a subtraction game with at most three moves and any seed, if p + x is an extension of the move set for every move x (p the period of the outcome sequence), then the outcome sequence is purely periodic. The source's extension criterion, applied at n + p, pulls the losing positions of the periodic tail backward into the start of the sequence; what remains is to exclude an extra early losing position. Such a position would force all of its forward neighbours to be winning in the periodic tail, and a new counting lemma (Lemma K: inclusion–exclusion on three translates of the set of losing residues, with matching singleton and pair counts and a pointwise triple inclusion) shows that this cannot happen when there are at most three moves. Lean proves the literal conjecture, the version with the hypothesis only for k = 1, a stronger pure-periodicity statement, and Lemma K; it also proves that the statement fails for four moves ({1,2,6,11}) and that Lemma K fails for {2,5,6,7}.

rows.title: Unboundedness conjecture for the 2-adic valuations of $b_m(n)$
rows.record_statement:
Let $b_m(n)$ be the sequence considered in the paper and let $m\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq2}$ be such that $m$ is not of the form $2^k-1$ for any $k\in\mathbb{N}_{+}$. **Unbounded valuation conjecture.** The sequence

$$
\bigl(\nu_2(b_m(n))\bigr)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}
$$

is unbounded. This is proposed as a generalization of the preceding valuation observations, with the excluded values $m=2^k-1$ forming a separate family. The paper gives no general proof.
rows.source: Maciej Gawron, Piotr Miska and Maciej Ulas, “Arithmetic properties of coefficients of power series expansion of _n=0^(1-x^2^n)^t (with an Appendix by Andrzej Schinzel)”, arXiv:1703.01955 (2017).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture is false, and not just at one value: for every m = 2^K(4^j + 1) − 1 with K ≥ 4 and j ≥ 1 (none of the form 2^k − 1), 32 never divides b_m(n), so ν₂(b_m(n)) ≤ 4 for all n; the same holds for m = 11. Here b_m(n) is the number of m-coloured binary partitions of n, the coefficient of x^n in the m-th power of the generating function of partitions into powers of 2. The proof reduces b_m(n) modulo 32 to a finite automaton reading the binary digits of n (from the Mahler functional equation (1 − x)H(x) = H(x²)), and handles all j at once by a second finite-state argument on pairs of digits of n and of the exponent, using a closed set of 31 polynomials. Lean defines binary partitions as partitions into powers of 2 (checked against the first values of OEIS A018819), proves the functional equation bridge, and checks the certificates in the kernel. Sobolewski and Ulas (Results Math. 2023) proved automaticity at each fixed modulus and stated that boundedness was not known for any admissible m.

rows.title: Sign-change conjecture for Birch–Erdős representation functions
rows.record_statement:
Let $f_{p,q}(n)$ be the Birch–Erdős representation function, with $p$ and $q$ relatively prime integers satisfying $q>p>2$. **Sign-change conjecture.** The sign of

$$
f_{p,q}(n+1)-f_{p,q}(n)
$$

changes infinitely often. The conjecture is presented as a possible example of the Chebyshev bias phenomenon; the source does not establish it.
rows.source: Yuchen Ding, Honghu Liu and Zi Wang, “Note on a theorem of Birch and Erdős”, arXiv:2503.11676 (2025).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds: for all coprime q > p > 2, the difference f_{p,q}(n+1) − f_{p,q}(n) is strictly positive for infinitely many n and strictly negative for infinitely many n, where f_{p,q}(n) counts the representations of n as a sum of distinct numbers p^a q^b. Infinitely many increases follow from the authors' Corollary 3 (f is unbounded). The new part is the decreases: if f were eventually nondecreasing, a comparison at roots of unity would force certain twisted products over pure powers to vanish, while the exact product over all roots of unity gives a uniform lower bound; the contradiction needs p > 2 (for p = 2 the authors prove that f is monotone). Lean defines f by the source's literal representation count and proves both infinitely many strict increases and infinitely many strict decreases, with non-vacuity checks.

rows.title: The cycle complement stable-set polynomial conjecture
rows.record_statement:
Let $C_n$ be the cycle graph on $n$ vertices, let $p(C_n;z)$ denote its perfectly matchable set polynomial, and let $\overline{h}^*(C_n;z)$ denote the normalized $h^*$-polynomial of the stable set polytope of the complement of $C_n$. **Cycle polynomial conjecture.** For all $n\geq 4$, 

$$
\overline{h}^*(C_n; z) = p(C_n; z) + \frac{1+(-1)^{n+1}}{2}z^{(n+1)/2}.
$$

The formula agrees with the explicitly computed even-cycle case and with the listed examples through $n=9$; the asserted general identity, particularly for odd cycles, remains open in the source.
rows.source: Robert Davis and Florian Kohl, “Perfectly Matchable Set Polynomials and h^*-polynomials for Stable Set Polytopes of Complements of Graphs”, arXiv:2207.14759 (2022).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds for every n ≥ 4. The even case is Davis and Kohl's own Corollary 3.14; the new case is odd n ≥ 5, where the stable set polytope of the complement of the odd cycle is not a lattice-point-friendly compressed polytope and has the extra rank facet. The proof counts the lattice points of the dilates directly from the known facet description of the antihole (Padberg): a greedy recursion around the cycle has a unique real cyclic fixed point; expanding the integer residual weights counts matchings of the cycle, which gives the perfectly matchable set polynomial, and the half-integral fixed points give the one extra monomial z^{(n+1)/2}; a rank-2 transfer matrix assembles the generating function. Lean proves the identity for all n ≥ 4, odd and even, from the lattice-point description of the dilated polytope, so it does not depend on the source's Corollary 3.14, and checks the source's Table 2 for n = 4..7.

rows.title: The derivation construction conjecture for transposed Poisson n-Lie algebras
rows.record_statement:
Let $n\geq 2$ be an integer. Let $(L,\cdot,[\cdot,\ldots,\cdot])$ be a **transposed Poisson $n$-Lie algebra**, and let $D$ be a derivation of both $(L,\cdot)$ and $(L,[\cdot,\ldots,\cdot])$. Define an $(n+1)$-ary operation

$$
\mu(a_1,\ldots,a_{n+1})=\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}(-1)^{i-1}D(a_i)[a_1,\ldots,\hat{a}_i,\ldots,a_{n+1}],
$$

where $\hat{a}_i$ denotes omission of the $i$-th entry. **Derivation construction conjecture.** Then $(L,\cdot,\mu(\cdot,\ldots,\cdot))$ is a transposed Poisson $(n+1)$-Lie algebra. This conjecture extends the known construction for transposed Poisson 2-Lie algebras and addresses the open question of constructing and classifying simple transposed Poisson $n$-Lie algebras. Its validity for arbitrary $n\geq 2$ and the stated derivations remains open.
rows.source: Farukh Mashurov, “On the transposed Poisson n-Lie algebras”, arXiv:2501.01714 (2025).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture is false at n = 3 over every field of characteristic 0. The counterexample is a transposed Poisson 3-Lie algebra M₃ given by an explicit multiplication and bracket table, extended to polynomials in one variable t, with the derivation D = d/dt; the 4-ary operation μ built from D and the bracket fails the generalized Jacobi (Filippov) identity, with an explicit nonzero defect. The idea is that D = d/dt on the polynomial extension turns the Filippov defect of μ into a polynomial identity (a 'strong condition' whose first argument is itself a bracket) that would have to hold in the base algebra, and the table is chosen so that this degree-seven specialization is nonzero. Huang, Chen, Chen and Ding proved the construction for strong transposed Poisson n-Lie algebras, and Mashurov showed by a free-algebra computation that the strong condition can fail, without producing a counterexample to the construction. Lean states the conjecture with the bracket as a function with multilinearity and skew-symmetry hypotheses, over any field of characteristic 0, and proves its negation.

rows.title: Hole-one-descent conjecture for generalized monotone triangles
rows.record_statement:
Let $A_{n,j}$ denote the number of alternating-sign matrices of size $n$ whose unique $1$ in the first row is in column $j$, and let $n\geq1$ and $i=1,\ldots,n-1$. **Hole-one-descent conjecture.** The identity

$$
\alpha(n+1;1,2,\ldots,i-1,i+1,i,i+1,\ldots,n)=-\sum_{j=1}^{n}(j-i)A_{n,j}
$$

should hold. The source proves the case $i=1$ and obtains part of the general decomposition, but explicitly says that the remaining contribution from two structural classes is an open problem.
rows.source: Lukas Riegler, “Generalized Monotone Triangles: an extended Combinatorial Reciprocity Theorem”, arXiv:1207.4437 (2012).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture holds for all n ≥ 1 and 1 ≤ i ≤ n − 1. Here α(n; k₁, …, kₙ) is the polynomial that counts monotone triangles with bottom row k₁ < … < kₙ, evaluated at a row with one descent. The proof finds a specific identity among four evaluations of α at neighbouring rows (the four-position identity W1) and certifies it with Fischer's operator formula, by the method of Fischer–Riegler's Lemmas 8.1–8.2; it turns each successive difference in i into a value of α at a row with a repeated entry, which equals the total number A_n of alternating sign matrices, and telescoping from Riegler's published case i = 1 gives the formula. Lean defines α by Fischer's operator formula, proves that it counts monotone triangles at strictly increasing rows, and proves the identity over the full printed range, with A_{n,j} given as α at the deletion rows (and, in a second endpoint, as monotone-triangle counts).
